intent: Keep a symmetric five-sensor row as a clean baseline so the Integrator's controller can be judged on a known platform. Next iteration I will consider changing sensor spacing (narrower for sharper bends, wider for line-loss recovery) and sensor forward offset, depending on where the race shows line loss or oscillation. I am not committing to a change yet. Expected result: finishing the oval, s-bend and slalom tracks with at most a few line-loss events, and a completion time under 3 s.
learning: Baseline only. Open hypotheses: (1) a forward sensor offset of about 0.06 m reduces line loss on bends compared with sensors near the axle; (2) a 12 mm footprint gives a cleaner signal than 16 mm on a 25 mm tape; (3) the mass and wheel track trade off between acceleration and turn stability. Please report which sensor readings drop out first on the slalom, since that will show whether the spacing is too wide.
rationale: Iteration 0 has no Integration Feedback and no Geometry Race Data, so this is a baseline built from the contract rather than from evidence. I chose five sensors in a symmetric row across the front of the robot. Five sensors span +/-0.04 m, which is wider than the 25 mm tape, so the line stays visible across small lateral offsets while the 12 mm footprint still fits inside the tape width. A forward offset of 0.06 m puts the sensors ahead of the axle so the controller sees the line before the wheels reach it, which should help on bends. A wheel track of 0.12 m and wheel radius of 0.03 m give a stable turn rate and enough ground speed for the 1.5 m/s average needed to finish in 3 s. A mass of 0.7 kg keeps acceleration high. Body width 0.12 m gives an off-track limit of 0.06 m (the floor), which leaves room for the line to drift without ending the run early. Expected result: completion on the development tracks with few line-loss events, with the main risk being oscillation on tight bends if the Integrator uses high gain. I have not yet tested whether this spacing is better or worse than a narrower or wider row.
